chapters.title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter XXX
paragraphs: The glow of the first fire that began on the second of September was watched from the various roads by the fleeing Muscovites and by the retreating troops, with many different feelings.

The Rostov family spent the night at Mytishchi, fourteen miles from Moscow. They had started so late on the first of September, the road had been so blocked by vehicles and troops, and so many things had been forgotten and servants sent back for them, that they decided to spend that night at a place just three miles outside Moscow. The next morning they woke late and were again delayed so often that they only got as far as Great Mytishchi. At ten o'clock that evening, the Rostov family and the wounded traveling with them were all distributed in the yards and huts of that large village. The Rostovs' servants and coachmen and the orderlies of the wounded officers, after seeing to their masters, had supper, fed the horses, and came out onto the porches.

In a neighboring hut lay Raevsky's adjutant with a fractured wrist. The terrible pain he suffered made him moan constantly and pitifully, and his moaning sounded dreadful in the darkness of the autumn night. He had spent the first night in the same yard as the Rostovs. The countess said she had been unable to close her eyes because of his moaning, and at Mytishchi she moved to a worse hut simply to be farther from the wounded man.

In the darkness of the night one of the servants noticed, above the high body of a coach standing before the porch, the small glow of another fire. One glow had long been visible and everybody knew it was Little Mytishchi burning—set on fire by Mamonov's Cossacks.
"But look here, brothers, there's another fire!" remarked an orderly.
All turned their attention to the glow.
"But they told us Little Mytishchi was set on fire by Mamonov's Cossacks."
"But that's not Mytishchi, it's farther away."
"Look, it must be in Moscow!"
Two of those watching went around to the other side of the coach and sat down on its steps.
"It's more to the left. Why, Little Mytishchi is over there, and this is right on the other side."
Several men joined the first two.
"See how it's flaring," said one. "That's a fire in Moscow: either in the Sushchevsky or the Rogozhsky quarter."
No one replied, and for some time they all gazed silently at the spreading flames of the second fire in the distance.
Old Daniel Terentich, the count's valet (as he was called), came up to the group and shouted at Mishka.
"What are you staring at, you good-for-nothing?... The count will be calling and there's nobody there; go and gather the clothes together."
"I only ran out to get some water," said Mishka.
"But what do you think, Daniel Terentich? Doesn't it look as if that glow is in Moscow?" remarked one of the footmen.
Daniel Terentich made no reply, and again for a long time they were all silent. The glow spread, rising and falling, farther and farther.
"God have mercy... It's windy and dry..." said another voice.
"Just look! See what it's doing now. O Lord! You can even see the crows flying. Lord have mercy on us sinners!"
"They'll put it out, don't worry!"

"Who's going to put it out?" Daniel Terentich, who had been silent till then, was heard to say. His voice was calm and deliberate. "Moscow it is, brothers," said he. "Mother Moscow, the white..." his voice faltered, and he gave way to an old man's sob.
And it was as if they had all only been waiting for this to understand the significance of the glow they were watching. Sighs were heard, words of prayer, and the sobbing of the count's old valet.

chapters.title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter XXXI
paragraphs: The valet, returning to the cottage, told the count that Moscow was burning. The count put on his dressing gown and went out to look. Sonya and Madame Schoss, who had not yet undressed, went out with him. Only Natasha and the countess remained in the room. Petya was no longer with the family—he had gone on with his regiment, which was heading for Troitsa.

The countess, hearing that Moscow was on fire, began to cry. Natasha, pale and with a fixed look, was sitting on the bench under the icons just where she had sat down on arriving, and paid no attention to her father's words. She was listening to the ceaseless moaning of the adjutant, three houses away.

"Oh, how terrible," said Sonya, returning from the yard chilled and frightened. "I believe the whole of Moscow will burn, there's an awful glow! Natasha, do look! You can see it from the window," she said to her cousin, evidently wishing to distract her mind.

But Natasha looked at her as if not understanding what was said to her and again fixed her eyes on the corner of the stove. She had been in this state of stupor since the morning, when Sonya—to the surprise and annoyance of the countess—had for some inexplicable reason found it necessary to tell Natasha of Prince Andrew's wound and his being with their party. The countess had seldom been so angry with anyone as she was with Sonya. Sonya had cried and begged forgiveness, and now, as if trying to make up for her mistake, paid constant attention to her cousin.
"Look, Natasha, how dreadfully it is burning!" said she.
"What's burning?" asked Natasha. "Oh, yes, Moscow."

And as if simply to get rid of Sonya without offending her, she turned her face to the window, looked out in such a way that it was obvious she could not see anything, and settled back into her former position.
"But you didn't see it!"
"Yes, I really did," Natasha replied in a voice that begged to be left in peace.
Both the countess and Sonya understood that, naturally, neither Moscow nor the burning of Moscow nor anything else could seem important to Natasha.

The count came back and lay down behind the partition. The countess went up to her daughter and touched her head with the back of her hand as she used to do when Natasha was ill, then touched her forehead with her lips as if to feel whether she was feverish, and finally kissed her.
"You're cold. You're trembling all over. You'd better lie down," said the countess.
"Lie down? All right, I will. I'll lie down at once," said Natasha.

When that morning Natasha had been told that Prince Andrew was seriously wounded and was traveling with their party, she had at first asked many questions: Where was he going? How was he wounded? Was it serious? Could she see him? But after she was told that she could not see him, that he was seriously wounded but that his life was not in danger, she stopped asking questions or speaking at all—evidently not believing what they told her, and convinced that no matter what she said, she would hear the same thing. All the way she had sat motionless in a corner of the coach with wide-open eyes, and the expression the countess knew so well and feared so much was in them. Now she sat in the same way on the bench where she had settled upon arriving. She was planning something and either deciding or had already decided something in her mind. The countess knew this, but what it might be she did not know, and this alarmed and tormented her.
"Natasha, undress, darling; lie down on my bed."
A bed had been made up on a bedstead for the countess only. Madame Schoss and the two girls were to sleep on some hay on the floor.

"No, Mama, I'll lie down here on the floor," Natasha replied irritably, and she went to the window and opened it. Through the open window the moans of the adjutant could be heard more clearly. She put her head out into the damp night air, and the countess saw her slim neck shaking with sobs and throbbing against the window frame. Natasha knew it was not Prince Andrew who was moaning. She knew Prince Andrew was in the same yard as themselves, in a part of the hut across the passage; but this dreadful incessant moaning made her sob. The countess exchanged a look with Sonya.
"Lie down, darling; lie down, my pet," said the countess, softly touching Natasha's shoulders. "Come, lie down."
"Oh, yes... I'll lie down at once," said Natasha, and began hurriedly undressing, tugging at the tapes of her petticoat.

When she had thrown off her dress and put on a dressing jacket, she sat down with her foot tucked under her on the bed made up on the floor, jerked her thin, rather short braid of hair to the front, and began rebraiding it. Her long, thin, practiced fingers rapidly unbraided, rebraided, and tied up her hair. Her head moved from side to side from habit, but her eyes, feverishly wide, stared fixedly ahead. When she was finished getting ready for the night, she sank gently onto the sheet spread over the hay on the side nearest the door.
"Natasha, you'd better lie in the middle," said Sonya.
"I'll stay here," muttered Natasha. "Do lie down," she added crossly, and buried her face in the pillow.

The countess, Madame Schoss, and Sonya undressed hastily and lay down. The small lamp in front of the icons was the only light left in the room. But in the yard there was a glow from the fire at Little Mytishchi, a mile and a half away, and through the night came the noise of people shouting at a tavern Mamonov's Cossacks had set up across the street, and the adjutant's unceasing moans could still be heard.

For a long time Natasha listened intently to the sounds coming from inside and outside the room and did not move. First she heard her mother praying and sighing and the creaking of her bed, then Madame Schoss's familiar whistling snore and Sonya's gentle breathing. Then the countess called to Natasha. Natasha did not answer.
"I think she's asleep, Mama," said Sonya softly.
After a short silence the countess spoke again, but this time no one replied.
Soon after that Natasha heard her mother's steady breathing. Natasha did not move, though her small bare foot, sticking out from under the quilt, was growing cold on the bare floor.

As if to celebrate a victory over everybody, a cricket chirped in a crack in the wall. A rooster crowed far off and another replied nearby. The shouting in the tavern had died down; only the moaning of the adjutant was heard. Natasha sat up.
"Sonya, are you asleep? Mama?" she whispered.

No one replied. Natasha rose slowly and carefully, crossed herself, and stepped cautiously on the cold and dirty floor with her slim, supple, bare feet. The floorboards creaked. Stepping cautiously from one foot to the other, she ran like a kitten the few steps to the door and grasped the cold door handle.
It seemed to her that something heavy was beating rhythmically against all the walls of the room: it was her own heart, sinking with alarm and terror and overflowing with love.

She opened the door and stepped across the threshold onto the cold, damp earthen floor of the passage. The cold she felt refreshed her. With her bare feet she touched a sleeping man, stepped over him, and opened the door into the part of the hut where Prince Andrew lay. It was dark in there. In the farthest corner, on a bench beside a bed on which something was lying, stood a tallow candle with a long, thick, smoldering wick.

From the moment she had been told that morning of Prince Andrew's wound and his presence there, Natasha had resolved to see him. She did not know why she had to, she knew the meeting would be painful, but felt all the more certain that it was necessary.

All day she had lived only in hope of seeing him that night. But now that the moment had come, she was filled with dread of what she might see. How was he disfigured? What was left of him? Was he like that incessant moaning of the adjutant? Yes, he was that moaning made flesh. When she saw an indistinct shape in the corner and mistook his knees raised under the quilt for his shoulders, she imagined a horrible body there and stood still in terror. But an irresistible impulse drew her forward. She cautiously took one step and then another, and found herself in the middle of a small room filled with baggage. Another man—Timokhin—was lying in a corner on the benches beneath the icons, and two others—the doctor and a valet—lay on the floor.

The valet sat up and whispered something. Timokhin, kept awake by the pain in his wounded leg, gazed with wide-open eyes at this strange apparition of a girl in a white nightdress, dressing jacket, and nightcap. The valet's sleepy, frightened exclamation—"What do you want? What's the matter?"—made Natasha approach more swiftly to what was lying in the corner. No matter how unlike a man that body looked, she had to see him. She passed the valet, the snuff fell from the candle wick, and she saw Prince Andrew clearly with his arms outside the quilt, and just as she had always known him.

He was the same as ever, but the feverish color of his face, his glittering eyes turned rapturously toward her, and especially his neck—delicate as a child's, revealed by the turned-down collar of his shirt—gave him a peculiarly innocent, childlike look, such as she had never seen on him before. She went up to him and with a swift, flexible, youthful movement dropped to her knees.
He smiled and held out his hand to her.

chapters.title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter XXXII
paragraphs: Seven days had passed since Prince Andrew found himself at the field hospital on the battlefield of Borodino. His feverish state and the inflammation of his injured bowels, the doctor believed, would certainly kill him. But on the seventh day he ate a piece of bread with some tea with pleasure, and the doctor noticed that his temperature was lower. He had regained consciousness that morning. The first night after they left Moscow had been fairly warm and he had remained in the carriage, but at Mytishchi the wounded man himself asked to be taken out and given some tea. The pain caused by being moved into the hut made him groan aloud and lose consciousness again. When he had been placed on his camp bed, he lay for a long time motionless with closed eyes. Then he opened them and whispered softly: "And the tea?" Remembering such a small, everyday detail astonished the doctor. He felt Prince Andrew's pulse and, to his surprise and dissatisfaction, found it had improved. He was dissatisfied because he knew from experience that if his patient did not die now, he would die a little later with greater suffering. Timokhin, the red-nosed major from Prince Andrew's regiment, had joined him in Moscow and was being taken along, having been wounded in the leg at Borodino. They were accompanied by a doctor, Prince Andrew's valet, his coachman, and two orderlies.
They gave Prince Andrew some tea. He drank it eagerly, looking with feverish eyes at the door before him as if trying to understand and remember something.
"I don't want any more. Is Timokhin here?" he asked.
Timokhin crept along the bench toward him.
"I am here, your excellency."
"How's your wound?"
"Mine, sir? All right. But how about you?"
Prince Andrew pondered again as if trying to remember something.
"Couldn't someone get me a book?" he asked.
"What book?"
"The Gospels. I don't have one."

The doctor promised to get it for him and began asking how he was feeling. Prince Andrew answered all his questions reluctantly but reasonably, then said he wanted a bolster placed under him because he was uncomfortable and in great pain. The doctor and valet lifted the cloak covering him and, making wry faces at the terrible smell of mortifying flesh that came from the wound, began examining that dreadful place. The doctor was very much displeased about something and made a change in the dressings, turning the wounded man over so that he groaned again and grew unconscious and delirious from the agony. He kept asking them to get him the book and put it under him.
"What trouble would it be to you?" he said. "I don't have one. Please get it for me and put it underneath for a moment," he pleaded in a piteous voice.
The doctor went into the passage to wash his hands.
"You people have no conscience," said he to the valet who was pouring water over his hands. "I turn my back for one moment... It's such pain, you know, I'm amazed he can bear it."
"By the Lord Jesus Christ, I thought we had put something under him!" said the valet.

The first time Prince Andrew understood where he was and what had happened, and remembered being wounded, was when he asked to be carried into the hut after his carriage had stopped at Mytishchi. After growing confused from pain while being carried in, he again regained consciousness, and while drinking tea once more recalled everything that had happened to him, and above all vividly remembered the moment at the field hospital when, at the sight of the suffering of a man he disliked, those new thoughts had come to him—thoughts that promised happiness. And those thoughts, though now vague and indefinite, again filled his soul. He remembered that he had a new source of happiness, and that this happiness had something to do with the Gospels. That was why he asked for a copy. The uncomfortable position they had put him in and turned him over again confused his thoughts, and when he came to himself a third time, it was in the complete stillness of the night. Everyone near him was sleeping. A cricket chirped from across the passage; someone was shouting and singing in the street; cockroaches rustled on the table, on the icons, and on the walls, and a big fly buzzed at the head of the bed and around the candle beside him, its wick charred and shaped like a mushroom.

His mind was not in a normal state. A healthy person usually thinks of, feels, and remembers countless things simultaneously, but has the power and will to select one sequence of thoughts or events on which to focus all his attention. A healthy person can tear himself away from the deepest reflections to say a polite word to someone who enters, and then return to his own thoughts. But Prince Andrew's mind was not in a normal state in that respect. All the powers of his mind were more active and clearer than ever, but they operated apart from his will. The most diverse thoughts and images occupied him simultaneously. At times his brain suddenly began to work with a vigor, clarity, and depth it had never reached when he was healthy, but suddenly in the midst of its work it would turn to some unexpected idea and he lacked the strength to return to the first.

"Yes, a new happiness was revealed to me—one that cannot be taken from a person," he thought as he lay in the semi-darkness of the quiet hut, gazing fixedly before him with feverish, wide-open eyes. "A happiness lying beyond material forces, beyond the material influences that act on a person—a happiness of the soul alone, the happiness of loving. Every person can understand it, but only God could conceive and command it. But how did God command that law? And why was the Son...?"

And suddenly the sequence of these thoughts broke off, and Prince Andrew heard (without knowing whether it was a delusion or reality) a soft whispering voice incessantly and rhythmically repeating "piti-piti-piti," and then "titi," and then again "piti-piti-piti," and "ti-ti" once more. At the same time he felt that above his face, above the very middle of it, some strange airy structure was being built out of slender needles or splinters, to the sound of this whispered music. He felt that he had to balance carefully (though it was difficult) so that this airy structure would not collapse; but nevertheless it kept collapsing and again slowly rising to the sound of the whispered rhythmic music—"it stretches, stretches, spreading out and stretching," said Prince Andrew to himself. While listening to this whispering and feeling the sensation of drawing out and the construction of this needle-like edifice, he also saw by glimpses a red halo around the candle, and heard the rustle of the cockroaches and the buzzing of the fly that bumped against his pillow and face. Each time the fly touched his face it gave him a burning sensation, and yet to his surprise it did not destroy the structure, though it hit the very spot where it was rising. But besides all this there was something else of importance. It was something white by the door—the statue of a sphinx, which also oppressed him.

"But perhaps that's my shirt on the table," he thought, "and those are my legs, and that is the door, but why is it always stretching and drawing itself out, and 'piti-piti-piti' and 'ti-ti' and 'piti-piti-piti'...? That's enough, please stop!" Prince Andrew painfully entreated someone. And suddenly thoughts and feelings again surfaced in his mind with peculiar clarity and force.

"Yes—love," he thought again quite clearly. "But not love that loves for something, for some quality, for some purpose, or for some reason, but the love which I—while dying—first experienced when I saw my enemy and yet loved him. I experienced that feeling of love which is the very essence of the soul and does not require an object. Now again I feel that bliss. To love one's neighbors, to love one's enemies, to love everything—to love God in all His forms. It is possible to love someone dear to you with human love, but an enemy can only be loved by divine love. That is why I experienced such joy when I felt that I loved that man. What has become of him? Is he alive?...

"When loving with human love one may pass from love to hatred, but divine love cannot change. No, neither death nor anything else can destroy it. It is the very essence of the soul. Yet how many people have I hated in my life? And of them all, I loved and hated none as I did her." And he vividly pictured Natasha to himself, not as he had done in the past with nothing but her charms which gave him pleasure, but for the first time picturing her soul. And he understood her feelings, her suffering, her shame, and her remorse. He now understood for the first time all the cruelty of his rejection of her, the cruelty of his break with her. "If only it were possible to see her once more! Just once, looking into those eyes to say..."

"Piti-piti-piti and ti-ti and piti-piti-piti boom!" buzzed the fly... And his attention was suddenly carried into another world, a world of reality and delirium in which something was happening. In that world some structure was still being built and did not fall, something was still stretching out, and the candle with its red halo was still burning, and the same shirt-like sphinx lay near the door; but besides all this something creaked, there was a breath of fresh air, and a new white sphinx appeared, standing at the door. And that sphinx had the pale face and shining eyes of the very Natasha of whom he had just been thinking.

"Oh, how oppressive this constant delirium is," thought Prince Andrew, trying to drive that face from his imagination. But the face remained before him with the force of reality and drew nearer. Prince Andrew wished to return to that former world of pure thought, but he could not, and delirium drew him back. The soft whispering voice continued its rhythmic murmur, something pressed on him and stretched out, and the strange face was before him. Prince Andrew gathered all his strength in an effort to recover his senses; he moved a little, and suddenly there was a ringing in his ears, a dimness in his eyes, and like a man plunged into water he lost consciousness. When he came to himself, Natasha—that same living Natasha whom of all people he most longed to love with this new, pure, divine love that had been revealed to him—was kneeling before him. He realized it was the real, living Natasha, and he was not surprised but quietly happy. Natasha, motionless on her knees (she could not move), with frightened eyes fixed on him, was holding back her sobs. Her face was pale and rigid. Only in the lower part of it something quivered.
Prince Andrew sighed with relief, smiled, and held out his hand.
"You?" he said. "How fortunate!"
With a quick but careful movement, Natasha drew closer to him on her knees and, taking his hand gently, bent her face over it and began kissing it, barely touching it with her lips.
"Forgive me!" she whispered, raising her head and glancing at him. "Forgive me!"
"I love you," said Prince Andrew.
"Forgive...!"
"Forgive what?" he asked.
"Forgive me for what I ha-ve do-ne!" Natasha faltered in a scarcely audible, broken whisper, and began kissing his hand more quickly, just touching it with her lips.
"I love you more, better than before," said Prince Andrew, lifting her face with his hand so he could look into her eyes.

Those eyes, filled with happy tears, gazed at him shyly, compassionately, and with joyous love. Natasha's thin pale face, with its swollen lips, was more than plain—it was awful. But Prince Andrew did not see that; he saw her shining eyes, which were beautiful. They heard the sound of voices behind them.

Peter the valet, now wide awake, had roused the doctor. Timokhin, who had not slept at all because of the pain in his leg, had long been watching everything, carefully covering his bare body with the sheet as he huddled on his bench.
"What's this?" said the doctor, rising from his bed. "Please go away, madam!"
At that moment a maid sent by the countess, who had noticed her daughter's absence, knocked at the door.
Like a sleepwalker awakened from her sleep, Natasha went out of the room and, returning to her hut, fell sobbing on her bed.

From that time on, during all the rest of the Rostovs' journey, at every stop and wherever they spent a night, Natasha never left the wounded Bolkonsky, and the doctor had to admit that he had not expected such firmness or such skill in nursing from a young girl.

Dreadful as the countess imagined it would be should Prince Andrew die in her daughter's arms during the journey—as, judging by what the doctor said, seemed possible—she could not oppose Natasha. Though with the intimacy now established between the wounded man and Natasha the thought occurred that should he recover their former engagement would be renewed, no one—least of all Natasha and Prince Andrew—spoke of this. The unsettled question of life and death, which hung not only over Bolkonsky but over all Russia, shut out every other consideration.

chapters.title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter XXXIII
paragraphs: On the third of September Pierre woke late. His head ached, the clothes in which he had slept without undressing felt uncomfortable on his body, and his mind held a dim awareness of something shameful he had done the day before. That something shameful was his conversation with Captain Ramballe.

It was eleven by the clock, but it seemed peculiarly dark outside. Pierre got up, rubbed his eyes, and seeing the engraved pistol which Gerasim had replaced on the writing table, remembered where he was and what lay before him that day.
"Am I too late?" he thought. "No, probably he won't enter Moscow before noon."
Pierre did not allow himself to think about what lay ahead, but hurried to act.

After adjusting his clothes, he took the pistol and was about to go out. But then it occurred to him for the first time that he certainly could not carry the weapon in his hand through the streets. It was hard to hide such a big pistol even under his wide coat. He could not carry it unnoticed in his belt or under his arm. Besides, it had been fired and he had not had time to reload it. "No matter, the dagger will do," he said to himself, though when planning his design he had more than once concluded that the chief mistake of the student who tried to kill Napoleon in 1809 was trying to do it with a dagger. But since his chief purpose was not really to carry out his plan, but to prove to himself that he would not abandon his intention and was doing everything he could to achieve it, Pierre hastily took the blunt, jagged dagger in a green sheath which he had bought with the pistol at the Sukharev market and hid it under his waistcoat.
Tying a belt over his coat and pulling his cap low on his head, Pierre went down the corridor, trying to avoid making noise or meeting the captain, and slipped out into the street.

The fire, which he had looked at so indifferently the evening before, had grown enormously during the night. Moscow was burning in several places. The buildings in Carriage Row, across the river, in the Bazaar and the Povarskoy, as well as the barges on the Moscow River and the timber yards by the Dorogomilov Bridge, were all ablaze.

Pierre's way led through side streets to the Povarskoy and from there to the church of St. Nicholas on the Arbat, where he had long before decided the deed should be done. The gates of most houses were locked and the shutters up. The streets and lanes were deserted. The air was full of smoke and the smell of burning. Now and then he met Russians with anxious, timid faces, and Frenchmen with a look not of the city but of the camp, walking in the middle of the streets. Both the Russians and the French looked at Pierre with surprise. Besides his height and stoutness, and the strange, gloomy look of suffering in his face and whole figure, the Russians stared at Pierre because they could not figure out what class he belonged to. The French followed him with astonishment mainly because Pierre, unlike all the other Russians who gazed at them with fear and curiosity, paid no attention to them. At the gate of one house, three Frenchmen who were trying to explain something to some Russians who did not understand them stopped Pierre and asked if he spoke French.

Pierre shook his head and went on. In another side street a sentinel beside a green ammunition wagon shouted at him, but only when the shout was repeated threateningly and he heard the click of the man's musket did Pierre understand that he had to cross to the other side of the street. He heard nothing and saw nothing of what went on around him. He carried his resolution within himself with terror and haste, like something dreadful and alien, for after the previous night's experience he was afraid of losing it. But he was not destined to bring his mood safely to its destination. And even had nothing hindered him along the way, his intention could not now have been carried out, for Napoleon had passed the Arbat more than four hours earlier on his way from the Dorogomilov suburb to the Kremlin, and was now sitting in a very gloomy mood in a royal study in the Kremlin, giving detailed orders for measures to extinguish the fire, prevent looting, and reassure the inhabitants. But Pierre did not know this; entirely absorbed in what lay before him, he was tortured—as are all those who stubbornly undertake a task impossible for them not because of its difficulty but because of its incompatibility with their nature—by the fear of weakening at the decisive moment and losing his self-respect.
Though he heard and saw nothing around him, he found his way by instinct and did not go wrong in the side streets leading to the Povarskoy.

As Pierre approached that street, the smoke became denser and denser—he could even feel the heat of the fire. Occasionally tongues of flame curled out from under the roofs of buildings. He met more people in the streets, and they were more agitated. But Pierre, though he sensed that something unusual was happening around him, did not realize he was approaching the fire. As he walked along a footpath across a wide-open space adjoining the Povarskoy on one side and the gardens of Prince Gruzinsky's house on the other, Pierre suddenly heard a woman's desperate weeping close to him. He stopped as if awakening from a dream and lifted his head.

By the side of the path, on the dusty dry grass, all sorts of household goods lay in a heap: featherbeds, a samovar, icons, and trunks. On the ground, beside the trunks, sat a thin woman no longer young, with long, prominent upper teeth, wearing a black cloak and cap. This woman, swaying back and forth and muttering something, was choking with sobs. Two girls of about ten and twelve, dressed in dirty short frocks and cloaks, were staring at their mother with stupefied, pale, frightened faces. The youngest child, a boy of about seven wearing an overcoat and an enormous cap that was obviously not his own, was crying in his old nurse's arms. A dirty, barefooted maid was sitting on a trunk, having undone her pale-colored braid, and was pulling it straight and sniffing at her singed hair. The woman's husband, a short, round-shouldered man in the undress uniform of a civilian official, with sausage-shaped whiskers and hair smoothly brushed forward over his temples under his square-set cap, was moving the trunks, which were placed one on another, and dragging some garments from under them, his face expressionless.
As soon as she saw Pierre, the woman almost threw herself at his feet.

"Dear people, good Christians, save me, help me, dear friends... help us, somebody," she sobbed. "My girl... My daughter! My youngest daughter was left behind. She's burned! Oh! Was it for this I nursed you... Oh!"
"Don't, Maria Nikolaevna!" said her husband to her in a low voice, evidently only to justify himself before the stranger. "Sister must have taken her, or else where can she be?" he added.

"Monster! Villain!" shouted the woman angrily, suddenly ceasing to weep. "You have no heart, you don't care about your own child! Another man would have rescued her from the fire. But this is a monster, not a man, not a father! You, honored sir, are a noble man," she went on, addressing Pierre rapidly between her sobs. "The fire broke out next door, and blew our way, the maid called out 'Fire!' and we rushed to grab our things. We ran out just as we were... This is what we saved... The icons, and my dowry bed, everything else is lost. We grabbed the children. But not Katie! Oh, Lord!..." and again she began to sob. "My child, my darling! Burned, burned!"
"But where was she left?" asked Pierre.
From the expression on his engaged face, the woman saw that this man might help her.

"Oh, dear sir!" she cried, seizing him by the legs. "My savior, give me some peace of mind... Aniska, go, you horrible girl, show him the way!" she cried to the maid, angrily opening her mouth and further exposing her long teeth.
"Show me the way, show me, I... I'll do it," gasped Pierre rapidly.

The dirty maid stepped from behind the trunk, put up her braid, sighed, and went on her short, bare feet along the path. Pierre felt as if he had come back to life after a heavy swoon. He held his head higher, his eyes shone with the light of life, and with swift steps he followed the maid, overtook her, and came out on the Povarskoy. The whole street was full of clouds of black smoke. Tongues of flame here and there broke through the clouds. A great number of people crowded in front of the fire. In the middle of the street stood a French general saying something to those around him. Pierre, accompanied by the maid, was heading toward the spot where the general stood, but the French soldiers stopped him.
"You can't pass!" cried a voice.
* "You can't pass!"
"This way, uncle," cried the girl. "We'll get through the side street, by the Nikulins'!"
Pierre turned back, breaking into a run now and then to keep up with her. She ran across the street, turned down a side street to the left, and passing three houses, turned into a yard on the right.

"It's here, right nearby," said she, and running across the yard, opened a gate in a wooden fence and, stopping, pointed out to him a small wooden wing of the house that was burning brightly and fiercely. One side had fallen in, another was on fire, and bright flames poured from the openings of the windows and from under the roof.
As Pierre passed through the fence gate, he was enveloped by hot air and involuntarily stopped.
"Which is it? Which is your house?" he asked.

"Ooh!" wailed the girl, pointing to the wing. "That's it, that was our home. You've burned to death, our darling, Katie, my precious little girl! Ooh!" lamented Aniska, who at the sight of the fire felt she too must express her feelings.

Pierre rushed to the wing, but the heat was so great that he involuntarily swerved in a curve and came upon the large house that was as yet burning only at one end, just below the roof, and around which swarmed a crowd of Frenchmen. At first Pierre did not realize what these men were doing, dragging things out; but seeing a Frenchman hitting a peasant with a flat saber, trying to take a fox-fur coat from him, he vaguely understood that looting was going on, though he had no time to dwell on the thought.

The sounds of crackling and the crash of falling walls and ceilings, the whistle and hiss of the flames, the excited shouts of the people, and the sight of the swaying smoke—now gathering into thick black clouds, now rising with glittering sparks, with here and there dense sheaves of flame (now red and now like golden fish scales creeping along the walls)—and the heat and smoke and speed of movement all produced on Pierre the usual stimulating effects of a fire. It had a particularly strong effect on him because at the sight of the fire he felt himself suddenly freed from the ideas that had weighed him down. He felt young, bright, nimble, and resolute. He ran around to the other side of the wing and was about to dash into the part still standing when just above his head he heard several voices shouting, then a cracking sound and the ring of something heavy falling close beside him.

Pierre looked up and saw at a window of the large house some Frenchmen who had just thrown out the drawer of a chest, filled with metal articles. Other French soldiers standing below went up to the drawer.
"What does this fellow want?" shouted one of them, referring to Pierre.
"There's a child in that house. Haven't you seen a child?" cried Pierre.

"What's he talking about? Get along!" said several voices, and one of the soldiers, evidently afraid Pierre might try to take some of the plate and bronzes in the drawer, moved threateningly toward him.
"A child?" shouted a Frenchman from above. "I did hear something squealing in the garden. Maybe it's his kid the fellow is looking for. After all, one must be humane, you know..."
"Where is it? Where?" said Pierre.
"There! There!" shouted the Frenchman at the window, pointing to the garden at the back of the house. "Wait a bit—I'm coming down."

And a minute or two later the Frenchman, a dark-eyed fellow with a spot on his cheek, in shirtsleeves, really did jump out of a ground-floor window and, clapping Pierre on the shoulder, ran with him into the garden.
"Hurry up, you others!" he called to his comrades. "It's getting hot."
When they reached a gravel path behind the house, the Frenchman pulled Pierre by the arm and pointed to a round, graveled space where a three-year-old girl in a pink dress was lying under a bench.

"There's your child! Oh, a girl, so much the better!" said the Frenchman. "Goodbye, Fatty. We must be humane—we're all mortal, you know!" and the Frenchman with the spot on his cheek ran back to his comrades.

Breathless with joy, Pierre ran to the little girl and was about to pick her up. But seeing a stranger, the sickly, scrofulous-looking child—unattractively like her mother—began to scream and run away. Pierre, however, seized her and lifted her in his arms. She screamed desperately and angrily, trying with her little hands to pull Pierre's hands away and to bite them with her slobbering mouth. Pierre was seized by a feeling of horror and revulsion, like touching some nasty little animal. But he made an effort not to drop the child and ran with her toward the large house. It was now impossible to get back the way he had come; the maid, Aniska, was no longer there, and Pierre, with a feeling of pity and disgust, pressed the wet, painfully sobbing child to himself as tenderly as he could and ran with her through the garden, looking for another way out.

chapters.title: Book Twelve (1812) — Chapter XXXIV
paragraphs: Having run through various yards and side streets, Pierre got back with his little burden to the Gruzinsky garden at the corner of the Povarskoy. He did not at first recognize the place from which he had set out to look for the child, so crowded was it now with people and goods that had been dragged out of the houses. Besides Russian families who had taken refuge here from the fire with their belongings, there were several French soldiers in various clothing. Pierre took no notice of them. He hurried to find the family of that civil servant in order to return the daughter to her mother and go save someone else. Pierre felt that he still had much to do and had to do it quickly. Glowing with the heat and from running, he felt at that moment more strongly than ever the sense of youth, energy, and determination that had come over him when he ran to save the child. She had now become quiet and, clinging with her little hands to Pierre's coat, sat on his arm gazing about her like some little wild animal. He glanced at her occasionally with a slight smile. He thought he saw something touchingly innocent in that frightened, sickly little face.

He did not find the civil servant or his wife where he had left them. He walked among the crowd with quick steps, scanning the various faces. Involuntarily he noticed a Georgian or Armenian family consisting of a very handsome old man of Eastern appearance wearing a new cloth-covered sheepskin coat and new boots, an old woman of similar type, and a young woman. That very young woman seemed to Pierre the perfection of Eastern beauty, with her sharply arched black eyebrows and the extraordinarily soft, bright color of her long, beautiful, expressionless face. Amid the scattered property and the crowd in the open space, she, in her rich satin cloak with a bright lilac shawl on her head, suggested a delicate exotic plant thrown onto the snow. She was sitting on some bundles a little behind the old woman, and looked from under her long lashes with motionless, large, almond-shaped eyes at the ground before her. Evidently she was aware of her beauty and fearful because of it. Her face struck Pierre, and hurrying along by the fence, he turned several times to look at her. When he had reached the fence, still without finding those he sought, he stopped and looked about him.
With the child in his arms, his figure was now more noticeable, and a group of Russians—both men and women—gathered around him.
"Have you lost someone, my dear fellow? You're a gentleman yourself, aren't you? Whose child is it?" they asked him.
Pierre replied that the child belonged to a woman in a black coat who had been sitting there with her other children, and he asked whether anyone knew where she had gone.
"Why, that must be the Anferovs," said an old deacon, addressing a pockmarked peasant woman. "Lord have mercy, Lord have mercy!" he added in his customary bass.
"The Anferovs? No," said the woman. "They left in the morning. That must be either Maria Nikolaevna's or the Ivanovs'!"
"He says 'a woman,' and Maria Nikolaevna is a lady," remarked a house servant.
"Do you know her? She's thin, with long teeth," said Pierre.
"That's Maria Nikolaevna! They went into the garden when these wolves swooped down," said the woman, pointing to the French soldiers.
"O Lord, have mercy!" added the deacon.
"Go over that way, they're there. It's her! She kept crying and carrying on," continued the woman. "It's her. Here, this way!"

But Pierre was not listening to the woman. He had for some seconds been intently watching what was happening a few steps away. He was looking at the Armenian family and at two French soldiers who had gone up to them. One of them, a quick little man, was wearing a blue coat tied round the waist with a rope. He had a nightcap on his head and his feet were bare. The other, whose appearance particularly struck Pierre, was a tall, lanky, round-shouldered, fair-haired man, slow in his movements and with a vacant expression. He wore a woman's loose gown of rough cloth, blue trousers, and large torn Hessian boots. The little barefooted Frenchman in the blue coat went up to the Armenians and, saying something, immediately seized the old man by his legs and the old man began pulling off his boots. The other, in the rough cloth gown, stopped in front of the beautiful Armenian girl and, with his hands in his pockets, stood staring at her, motionless and silent.

"Here, take the child!" said Pierre urgently and hurriedly to the woman, handing the little girl to her. "Give her back to them, give her back!" he almost shouted, putting the screaming child on the ground, and turning back to look at the Frenchman and the Armenian family.

The old man was already sitting barefoot. The little Frenchman had secured his second boot and was slapping one boot against the other. The old man was saying something in a voice broken by sobs, but Pierre caught only a glimpse of this—his whole attention was on the Frenchman in the rough gown, who meanwhile, swaying slowly from side to side, had drawn nearer to the young woman and, taking his hands from his pockets, had seized her by the neck.
The beautiful Armenian still sat motionless and in the same position, with her long lashes drooping as if she did not see or feel what the soldier was doing to her.

While Pierre was running the few steps that separated him from the Frenchman, the tall marauder in the rough gown was already tearing the necklace from the young Armenian woman's neck, and the young woman, clutching at her throat, screamed piercingly.
"Leave that woman alone!" Pierre exclaimed hoarsely in a furious voice, seizing the soldier by his round shoulders and throwing him aside.
The soldier fell, got up, and ran away. But his comrade, dropping the boots and drawing his sword, moved threateningly toward Pierre.
"Look here, no nonsense!" he cried.
* "Look here, no nonsense!"

Pierre was in such a transport of rage that he remembered nothing, and his strength increased tenfold. He rushed at the barefooted Frenchman and, before the latter could draw his sword, knocked him off his feet and hammered him with his fists. Shouts of approval were heard from the crowd around, and at the same moment a mounted patrol of French Uhlans appeared from around the corner. The Uhlans came up at a trot to Pierre and the Frenchman and surrounded them. Pierre remembered nothing of what happened after that. He only remembered beating someone and being beaten, and finally feeling that his hands were bound and that a crowd of French soldiers stood around him, searching him.
"Lieutenant, he has a dagger," were the first words Pierre understood.

"Ah, a weapon?" said the officer, and turned to the barefooted soldier who had been arrested with Pierre. "All right, you can tell all about it at the court-martial." Then he turned to Pierre. "Do you speak French?"

Pierre looked around him with bloodshot eyes and did not reply. His face probably looked very terrible, for the officer said something in a whisper and four more Uhlans left the ranks and positioned themselves on both sides of Pierre.
"Do you speak French?" the officer asked again, keeping his distance from Pierre. "Call the interpreter."
A small man in Russian civilian clothes rode out from the ranks, and by his clothes and manner of speaking Pierre at once recognized him as a French salesman from one of the Moscow shops.
"He doesn't look like a common man," said the interpreter, after giving Pierre a searching look.
"Ah, he looks very much like an arsonist," remarked the officer. "And ask him who he is," he added.
"Who are you?" asked the interpreter in poor Russian. "You must answer the chief."
"I will not tell you who I am. I am your prisoner—take me!" Pierre suddenly replied in French.
"Ah, ah!" muttered the officer with a frown. "Well then, march!"
A crowd had gathered around the Uhlans. Nearest to Pierre stood the pockmarked peasant woman with the little girl, and when the patrol started she moved forward.
"Where are they taking you, you poor dear?" said she. "And the little girl, the little girl—what am I supposed to do with her if she's not theirs?" said the woman.
"What does that woman want?" asked the officer.
Pierre was as if intoxicated. His exhilaration increased at the sight of the little girl he had saved.

"What does she want?" he murmured. "She is bringing me my daughter whom I have just saved from the flames," said he. "Goodbye!" And without knowing how this pointless lie had escaped him, he walked on with resolute, triumphant steps between the French soldiers.

The French patrol was one of those sent out through the various streets of Moscow by Durosnel's order to put a stop to the pillaging, and especially to catch the arsonists who, according to the prevailing opinion among the higher French officers, were the cause of the fires. After marching through a number of streets, the patrol arrested five more Russian suspects: a small shopkeeper, two seminary students, a peasant, and a house servant, besides several looters. But of all these various suspected characters, Pierre was considered the most suspicious of all. When they had all been brought for the night to a large house on the Zubov Rampart that was being used as a guardhouse, Pierre was placed apart under strict guard.
